nameStory: The Burred Horsehair Lichen gets its name from its dark, wiry strands that look remarkably like coarse horse hair hanging from tree branches. The "burred" part refers to the tiny bumps and projections along its surface, like tiny burrs that might cling to a horse's mane after a wild ride through the woods.
description: This distinctive lichen hangs in dark, stringy masses from tree branches like nature's own gothic decoration. The thin, hair-like strands are typically dark brown to blackish and can grow several inches long, creating drooping curtains on their host trees. Unlike many lichens that form crusts or leafy patches, this species has a distinctly three-dimensional, fruticose (shrubby) growth form that makes it easy to spot from a distance.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Long, thin strands that hang freely from branches like dark hair or fishing line, often in dense clusters that sway gently in the breeze

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark brown to nearly black when dry, may appear slightly greener when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Rough to the touch with tiny bumps and projections (the 'burrs') that you can feel when you gently run the strands between your fingers

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on coniferous trees, particularly spruces and firs, usually on older branches in the canopy

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual strands typically 2-6 inches long but can reach up to 8 inches, with clusters forming impressive hanging masses

habitat: Look for this lichen in mature coniferous forests throughout New England's mountains and cooler regions, particularly in areas with clean air and high humidity. It thrives on spruce and fir trees at higher elevations where morning fog and mist provide regular moisture. You'll most often spot it in old-growth or mature second-growth forests where the air quality is good enough to support these sensitive organisms.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more noticeable as it absorbs moisture from spring rains and fog, appearing darker and more pliable. This is an excellent time to feel the texture differences between wet and dry specimens.
seasonality.summer: May appear somewhat faded and brittle during dry spells, but remains visible hanging from branches. Look for it in shaded, humid spots where it retains more moisture.
seasonality.fall: Often most photogenic against autumn foliage, creating striking contrast with colorful deciduous trees in mixed forests. The lichen remains unchanged while the forest transforms around it.
seasonality.winter: Easily spotted against snow-covered branches, appearing as dark tangles. Winter is actually ideal for lichen observation since there are no leaves to obscure your view of tree branches.

funFact: This lichen can actually be used as a natural barometer - when humidity rises before a storm, the strands become noticeably more flexible and darker in color, sometimes serving as an early weather predictor for observant hikers!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Horsehair Lichen (Bryoria trichodes), but Burred Horsehair Lichen feels distinctly rougher and bumpier to the touch - run both between your fingers and you'll immediately feel the difference. Remember: 'Burred = Bumpy' for an easy memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: Like many hair lichens, this species is extremely sensitive to air pollution and serves as a natural indicator of forest health. Its presence suggests clean, unpolluted air, making it a welcomed sight for both ecologists and nature lovers who value pristine environments.
compareHints: Compared to its close relatives, Burred Horsehair Lichen has the roughest, most textured surface - you can actually feel the tiny projections. Horsehair Lichen is smoother to the touch, while Spiny Gray Horsehair Lichen tends to be lighter in color and has a different branching pattern. The tactile test is your best friend when identifying species in this tricky genus.
